document.title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Douglas Feith, "Strategy," with Attachment "U.S. Strategy in Afghanistan" (NSC, Oct 16, 2001)
document.authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld); attachment by National Security Council
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
document.note: [Secret] Foundational document for the first phase of U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, approved by the NSC on Oct 16, 2001, with Rumsfeld's handwritten edits and an Oct 30 cover note to Feith. It stresses destroying al-Qaeda and the Taliban, using any and all Afghan tribes and factions, inserting CIA teams and special forces, and avoiding commitment to post-Taliban military involvement. Diplomacy with Pakistan, Iran and Russia is emphasized, while UN diplomacy is limited.

events.description: NSC/DoD draft memo 'U.S. Strategy in Afghanistan' dated 7:43 AM setting goals against Al-Qaida and the Taliban.
Rumsfeld snowflake to Feith asking for edits to strategy paper before sending to Vice President, Powell, Rice and Tenet.
Draft discussion paper 'U.S. Strategy in Afghanistan' written setting goals re Al-Qaida and Taliban, execution, operations, Kabul plan.
Rumsfeld sends Feith edits to the strategy paper and a draft cover memo to the Vice President with copies to Powell, Rice and Tenet.
Proposed urgent insertion of additional CIA teams and Special Forces A teams into Afghanistan, North and South.
Proposed Northern Alliance advance to eliminate Taliban resistance in Kabul and take the city, with U.S. conventional support north of Kabul.

key_claims: US strategy aimed to eliminate Al-Qaida leadership and forces and end Taliban rule, treating both as people-based assets to be destroyed.
The paper proposed using any Afghan tribes and factions, with DoD and CIA coordination and incentives, to eliminate Al-Qaida and Taliban.
It called for urgent insertion of CIA teams and Special Forces in North and South, with the Northern Alliance advancing on Kabul.
It advised against committing to post-Taliban military involvement and against agonizing over post-Taliban arrangements.
It identified Pakistan as potentially key to establishing southern contacts to balance Northern Alliance gains.
It suggested exploring ties with King Zahir Shah and being wary of association with Russia and Iran given Pashtun fears.
It envisioned an international peacekeeping force for Kabul, not US-led, to relieve Pashtun fears of Northern Alliance domination.
